thread_analysis.thread_summary: Toytec Corporation (contact Takashi Kurokawa, later joined by a colleague Teramon-san) engages Allion (Itsuo Sakai, Masaya Iida, Toshitaka Mochizuki, lab engineer Kousuke Nakayama) for Bluetooth SIG certification testing, spanning September through late October 2024. The thread covers RF/RF PHY test scope tiering (1M/2M/Coded combinations, BR/EDR/BLE type changes, Stable Modulation Index test economics), test setup logistics (USB-UART cabling), and an extended RF PHY DTM troubleshooting saga whose root cause was a customer-referenced auxiliary tool (FCC_assist1.0.4.exe) conflicting with the lab's own InterLab test system over the same COM port -- a lab-side, not DUT-side, problem. This thread substantially overlaps with thread_0027's more internal capture of the same troubleshooting incident.
all_questions_found: Is 1M-only RF PHY testing sufficient, and what do the various PHY-mode test scope tiers cost? (see thread_0028_case_01)
What are the Stable Modulation Index Transmitter/Receiver test items, and is it worth testing them? (see thread_0028_case_02)
Can a customer-provided USB-UART module be extended over 1 meter, and is RF tester hardware the customer's responsibility? (see thread_0028_case_03)
Why does RF PHY testing consistently fail to get a normal DUT command response despite independent confirmation the DUT itself is healthy? (see thread_0028_case_04)

(Administrative, not separately cased) BR/EDR/BLE Support RF type change cost re-quotation, multi-site (Taiwan/Japan) test scheduling, SIG Qualification Fee wire transfer confirmation, and Class 2/3 test scope confirmation -- routine project administration without a generalizable technical lesson beyond what's captured in the cases above.
thread_analysis.key_technical_discussion: The thread's standout contribution is case_04's root-cause discovery: a persistent RF PHY DTM failure that looked like a DUT problem (surviving sample replacement and independent customer-side confirmation) turned out to be a COM-port conflict on the lab's own test system, caused by running an auxiliary tool intended for a different certification regime (radio-law/FCC) immediately before the actual SIG DTM test. Case_02's explanation of Stable Modulation Index economics (the test outcome is chipset-determined and not actionable via retesting) is also a clear, reusable scoping lesson.
thread_analysis.key_decision_logic: See thread_0028_case_01 through thread_0028_case_04 for case-specific decision logic; the throughline is matching test scope to actual product capability (case_01, case_02) and correctly isolating whether a persistent test failure originates from the DUT or from the lab's own test setup (case_04).
thread_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: See individual case files; case_04 carries the highest risk -- continuing to treat the persistent failure as DUT-side without identifying the COM-port tool conflict would have wasted further shipping cycles indefinitely.
thread_analysis.consulting_mistake: The lab's own test engineer caused the root-cause issue in case_04 by installing and running a customer-referenced auxiliary tool (FCC_assist1.0.4.exe) on the same control PC and COM port InterLab needed, without recognizing the conflict -- this was acknowledged directly to the customer as 'our own basic mistake' once identified.
thread_analysis.consulting_takeaway: When a persistent DTM test failure survives sample replacement and independent confirmation that the DUT itself is healthy, look for a tooling conflict on the lab's own test system (e.g., two tools contending for the same COM port) before continuing to suspect the DUT; and when scoping RF PHY tests, transparently present cost-tier tradeoffs and flag tests (like Stable Modulation Index) whose outcome is effectively predetermined by an unchangeable product characteristic.
